contenido: 1. The effort aimed at announcing the Gospel to the men of our time, exalted by hope but at the same time frequently disturbed by fear and anguish, is without a doubt a service that is presented to the Christian community and even to all of humanity.

2. This is what we wish to do now, at the end of the Holy Year, during which the Church has strived to announce the Gospel to all men, however with no other objective than to fulfill its duty as messenger of the Good News of Jesus Christ proclaimed based on two fundamental slogans: "put on the new man" and "be reconciled to God."

3. On various occasions, already before the Synod, We highlighted the importance of this theme of evangelization. "The conditions of society," we said to the Sacred College of Cardinals on June 22, 1973, "oblige us, therefore, to review methods, to seek by all means the way to bring the Christian message to modern man, in which only he can find the answer to his questions and the strength for his commitment to human solidarity." And we added that, to give a valid response to the demands of the Council that are pressing upon us, we absolutely need to get in touch with the heritage of faith that the Church has the duty to preserve in all its purity, and at the same time the duty to present it to the men of our time, with the means at our disposal, in an understandable and persuasive way.

4. This fidelity to a message of which we are servants, and to the people to whom we must transmit it intact and alive, is the central axis of evangelization. This raises three pressing questions, which the Synod of 1974 has constantly kept in mind: âHow effective is the hidden energy of the Good News in our days, capable of profoundly shaking the conscience of man? âTo what extent and how can this evangelical force truly transform the man of today? âWith what methods must the Gospel be proclaimed so that its power is effective? These questions develop, in essence, the fundamental question that the Church proposes today and which could be stated as follows: after the Council and thanks to the Council that has constituted for her an hour of God in this cycle of history, is the Church more or less capable of announcing the Gospel and inserting it into the heart of man with conviction, freedom of spirit and effectiveness?
5. We all see the urgent need to give such a question an answer, loyal, humble, brave, and to act accordingly.

6. The testimony that the Lord gives of Himself and that Saint Luke has collected in his Gospel "He must also announce the kingdom of God in other cities", undoubtedly has great scope, since it defines the entire mission of Jesus in a single phrase: "because for this purpose I have been sent." These words achieve their full meaning when considered in the light of the preceding verses in which Christ applies to Himself the words of the prophet Isaiah: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to evangelize the poor."

7. During the Synod, the bishops frequently recalled this truth: Jesus himself, the Gospel of God, was the first and greatest evangelizer. He has been until the end, until perfection, until the sacrifice of his earthly existence.

8. Christ, as evangelizer, announces above all a kingdom, the kingdom of God, so important that, in relation to it, everything becomes "the rest", which is given in addition. Only the kingdom is therefore absolute and all the rest is relative. The Lord will be pleased to describe in very different ways the joy of belonging to that kingdom, a paradoxical joy made of things that the world rejects, the demands of the kingdom and its Magna Carta, the heralds of the kingdom, its mysteries, its children, the vigilance and fidelity required of those who await its definitive arrival.

9. As the nucleus and center of his Good News, Jesus announces salvation, that great gift of God that is liberation from everything that oppresses man, but above all it is liberation from sin and the evil one, within the joy of knowing God and being known by Him, of seeing Him, of surrendering to Him. All this has its beginning during the life of Christ, and is definitively achieved by his death and resurrection; but it must be continued patiently through history until it is fully realized on the day of the final coming of Christ Himself, which no one knows when will take place except the Father.

10. This kingdom and this salvation – key words in the evangelization of Jesus Christ – can be received by every man, as grace and mercy; but at the same time each one must conquer them with force, "the kingdom of heaven is in tension and the strong snatch it away," says the Lord, with fatigue and suffering, with a life in accordance with the Gospel, with renunciation and the cross, with the spirit of the beatitudes. But, above all, each one achieves them through a total interior change, which the Gospel calls metanoia, a radical conversion, a profound transformation of the mind and heart.

11. Christ carried out this proclamation of the kingdom of God, through the tireless preaching of a word, of which it will be said that it admits of no comparison with any other: "What is this? A new doctrine clothed with authority"; "Everyone approved of him, marveling at the gracious words that came out of his mouth..."; "No man ever spoke like this." His words reveal the secret of God, his design and his promise, and therefore change the heart of man and his destiny.

12. But He also carries out this proclamation of salvation through innumerable signs that provoke astonishment in the crowds and that at the same time draw them towards Him to see Him, hear Him and allow themselves to be transformed by Him: sick people healed, water turned into wine, bread multiplied, the dead coming back to life and, above all, His own resurrection. And at the center of everything, the sign to which He attributes great importance: the little ones, the poor are evangelized, they become his disciples, they gather "in his name" in the great community of those who believe in him. Because the Jesus who declares: "I must also announce the kingdom of God in other cities, for that is why I was sent," is the same Jesus of whom John the Evangelist said that he had come and must die "to gather into one all the children of God, who are scattered." Thus He ends His revelation, completing and confirming it, with the manifestation made of Himself, with words and works, with signs and miracles, and in a particular way with His death, His resurrection and the sending of the Spirit of Truth.

13. Those who sincerely welcome the Good News, through such acceptance and participation in faith, gather together in the name of Jesus to seek the kingdom together, build it, live it. They constitute a community that is at the same time evangelizing. The order given to the Twelve: "Go and proclaim the Good News", also applies, although in a different way, to all Christians. For this reason Peter defines them as "a people acquired to proclaim the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light." These are the wonders that each one has been able to hear in their own language. Furthermore, the Good News of the kingdom that is coming and that has already begun, is for all men of all times. Those who have already received it and who are gathered in the community of salvation, can and must communicate and spread it.

14. The Church knows it. She is keenly aware that the words of the Savior: "I must also announce the kingdom of God in other cities," apply with complete truth to herself. And for her part she willingly adds, following Saint Paul: "Because, if I evangelize, it is not a reason for my glory, but rather it is imposed on me as a necessity. Woe to me if I do not evangelize!" With great joy and consolation, at the end of the October 1974 Assembly, We heard these luminous words: "We want to confirm once again that the task of evangelization of all men constitutes the essential mission of the Church"; a task and mission that the broad and profound changes in today's society make increasingly urgent. Evangelizing constitutes, in effect, the joy and vocation of the Church, its deepest identity. She exists to evangelize, that is, to preach and teach, to be a channel of the gift of grace, to reconcile sinners with God, to perpetuate the sacrifice of Christ in the holy Mass, memorial of his death and glorious resurrection.

15. Whoever reads the origins of the Church in the New Testament and follows her history step by step, who sees her live and act, realizes that she is linked to evangelization in the most intimate way:

16. There is, therefore, an intimate link between Christ, the Church and evangelization. While this time of the Church lasts, it is she who is in charge of the task of evangelizing. A task that cannot be accomplished without it, much less against it.

17. In the evangelizing action of the Church, some elements and aspects certainly come into play that must be kept in mind. Some are of such importance that there is a tendency to identify them simply with evangelization. Hence it has been possible to define evangelization in terms of announcing Christ to those who ignore him, preaching, catechesis, baptism and administration of the other sacraments.

18. Evangelizing means for the Church to bring the Good News to all areas of humanity and, with its influence, transform from within, renew humanity itself: "Behold, I make all things new." But the truth is that there is no new humanity if there are not, first of all, new men with the newness of baptism and life according to the Gospel. The purpose of evangelization is therefore this interior change and, if it had to be summarized in one word, it would be best to say that the Church evangelizes when, by the sole divine force of the Message it proclaims, it tries to convert at the same time the personal and collective conscience of men, the activity in which they are engaged, their concrete life and environment.

19. Sectors of humanity that are transformed: for the Church it is not only a matter of preaching the Gospel in increasingly vast geographical areas or increasingly numerous populations, but of reaching and transforming with the force of the Gospel the criteria of judgment, the determining values, the points of interest, the lines of thought, the inspiring sources and the life models of humanity, which are in contrast with the word of God and with the plan of salvation.

20. Possibly, we could express all this by saying: what matters is to evangelize – not in a decorative way, like a superficial varnish, but in a vital way, in depth and to its very roots – the culture and cultures of man in the rich and broad sense that its terms have in Gaudium et spes, always taking the person as a starting point and always keeping in mind the relationships of people among themselves and with God.

21. The Good News must be proclaimed first, through testimony. Let us suppose a Christian or a group of Christians who, within the human community where they live, manifest their capacity for understanding and acceptance, their communion of life and destiny with others, their solidarity in the efforts of all insofar as there is noble and good. Let us further suppose that they simply and spontaneously radiate their faith in values ​​that go beyond current values, and their hope in something that cannot be seen nor would they dare to dream. Through this wordless testimony, these Christians make those who contemplate their lives ask irresistible questions: Why are they like this? Why do they live that way? What or who inspires you? Why are they with us? Well, this testimony in itself constitutes a silent, but also very clear and effective proclamation of the Good News. There is in this an initial gesture of evangelization. These are possibly the first questions that many non-Christians will ask themselves, whether they are people to whom Christ had never been announced, non-practicing baptized people, people who live in a Christian society but according to non-Christian principles, or whether they are people who are searching, not without suffering, for something or Someone that they guess but without being able to give it a name. Other questions will arise, deeper and more compromising, provoked by this testimony that involves presence, participation, solidarity and that is an essential element, generally the first absolutely in evangelization.

22. And yet, this is still insufficient, since the most beautiful testimony will prove impotent in the long run if it is not clarified, justified - what Peter called giving "a reason for your hope" - made explicit by a clear and unequivocal announcement of the Lord Jesus. The Good News proclaimed by the testimony of life must therefore, sooner or later, be proclaimed by the word of life. There is no true evangelization until the name, doctrine, life, promises, kingdom, and mystery of Jesus of Nazareth, Son of God, are announced.

23. Indeed, the announcement only acquires its full dimension when it is heard, accepted, assimilated and when it gives rise to heartfelt adhesion in those who have received it. Adherence to the truths that the Lord has revealed in his mercy, it is true. But, even more so, adhesion to the life program â€œlife in reality already transformedâ€ that he proposes. In a word, adherence to the kingdom, that is, to the "new world", to the new state of things, to the new way of being, of living together, inaugurated by the Gospel. Such adhesion, which cannot remain something abstract and disembodied, is revealed concretely through a visible entry into a community of faithful. Thus, those whose lives have been transformed enter a community that is itself a sign of transformation, a sign of the newness of life: the Church, the visible sacrament of salvation. But at the same time, entry into the ecclesial community will be expressed through many other signs that prolong and display the sign of the Church. In the dynamism of evangelization, he who welcomes the Gospel as a saving Word normally translates it into these sacramental gestures: adhesion to the Church, acceptance of the sacraments that manifest and sustain this adhesion, by the grace they confer.

24. Finally, he who has been evangelized evangelizes in turn. Here is the proof of truth, the touchstone of evangelization: it is unthinkable that a man has accepted the Word and given himself to the kingdom without becoming someone who in turn witnesses and announces.

25. In the message announced by the Church there are certainly many secondary elements, the presentation of which depends largely on changes in circumstances. Such elements change too. But there is an essential content, a living substance, that cannot be modified or ignored without seriously denaturalizing evangelization itself.

26. It is not superfluous to remember: evangelizing is, above all, bearing witness, in a simple and direct way, to God revealed by Jesus Christ through the Holy Spirit. Testify that he has loved the world in his Incarnate Word, has given being to all things and has called men to eternal life. For many, it is possible that this testimony of an unknown God, whom they worship without giving him a specific name, or whom they seek because they feel a secret call in the heart, experiencing the emptiness of all idols. But this testimony is fully evangelizing when it shows that for man the Creator is not an anonymous and distant power: he is Father. "We are called children of God, and indeed we are" and, therefore, we are brothers one to another, in God.

27. Evangelization must also always contain – as the basis, center and at the same time the culmination of its dynamism – a clear proclamation that in Jesus Christ, Son of God made man, dead and resurrected, salvation is offered to all men, as a gift of God's grace and mercy. Not a purely immanent salvation, tailored to the material or even spiritual needs that are exhausted in the framework of temporal existence and are totally identified with temporal desires, hopes, issues and struggles, but a salvation that goes beyond all these limits to be realized in a communion with the only Absolute God, a transcendent, eschatological salvation, which certainly begins in this life, but which has its fulfillment in eternity.

28. Consequently, evangelization cannot but include the prophetic announcement of a beyond, a deep and definitive vocation of man, in continuity and discontinuity at the same time with the present situation: beyond time and history, beyond the reality of that world, whose hidden dimension will manifest one day; beyond man himself, whose true destiny is not exhausted in its temporal dimension but will be revealed to us in the future life. Evangelization also includes the preaching of hope in the promises made by God through the new covenant in Jesus Christ; the preaching of God's love for us and our love for God, the preaching of fraternal love for all men - the capacity for donation and forgiveness, for renunciation, for helping one's brother - which, because it comes from the love of God, is the core of the Gospel; the preaching of the mystery of evil and the active search for good. Preaching, likewise, and this becomes increasingly urgent, of the search for God himself through prayer, especially adoration and thanksgiving, and also through communion with that visible sign of the encounter with God that is the Church of Jesus Christ; communion that in turn is expressed through participation in those other signs of Christ, living and operating in the Church, which are the sacraments. Living the sacraments in this way until achieving true plenitude in their celebration is not, as some claim, placing an obstacle or accepting a deviation from evangelization: it is giving it all its integrity. Because the entirety of evangelization, apart from the preaching of the message, consists of establishing the Church, which does not exist without this respite from sacramental life culminating in the Eucharist.

29. Evangelization would not be complete if it did not take into account the reciprocal interpellation that in the course of time is established between the Gospel and the concrete, personal and social life of man. Precisely for this reason, evangelization carries with it an explicit message, adapted to different situations and constantly updated, about the rights and duties of every human person, about family life without which personal progress is hardly possible, about the community life of society, about international life, peace, justice, development; a message, especially powerful in our days, about liberation.

30. It is well known in what terms numerous bishops from all continents and, above all, the bishops of the Third World spoke during the recent Synod, with a pastoral accent in which the voices of millions of children of the Church who make up such peoples vibrated. People, we already know, committed with all their energies to the effort and struggle to overcome everything that condemns them to remain on the margins of life: hunger, chronic illnesses, illiteracy, impoverishment, injustice in international relations and, especially, in commercial exchanges, situations of economic and cultural neocolonialism, sometimes as cruel as the political one, etc. The Church, the bishops repeat, has the duty to announce the liberation of millions of human beings, among whom there are many of her children; the duty to help this liberation be born, to bear witness to it, to make it total. All this is not strange to evangelization.

31. Between evangelization and human promotion ( [+[0]+] ) there are indeed very strong ties. Links of an anthropological order, because the man who must be evangelized is not an abstract being, but a being subject to social and economic problems. Ties of a theological order, since the plan of creation cannot be dissociated from the plan of redemption that reaches very specific situations of injustice, which must be fought and justice that must be restored. Bonds of an eminently evangelical order such as that of charity: in fact, how can we proclaim the new commandment without promoting, through justice and peace, the true, authentic growth of man? We indicate this ourselves, remembering that it is not possible to accept "that the work of evangelization can or should forget the extremely serious issues, so agitated today, that concern justice, liberation, development and peace in the world. If this were to happen, it would be to ignore the doctrine of the Gospel about love for one's neighbor who suffers or is in need."

32. There is no reason to hide, in fact, that many generous Christians, sensitive to the dramatic questions that the problem of liberation entails, in wanting to involve the Church in the liberation effort, have often felt the temptation to reduce their mission to the dimensions of a purely temporal project; to reduce its objectives to an anthropocentric perspective; salvation, of which she is the messenger and sacrament, to material well-being; their activity “forgetting all spiritual and religious concerns” to political or social initiatives. If this were so, the Church would lose its deepest significance. Its message of liberation would have no originality and would lend itself to being monopolized and manipulated by ideological systems and political parties. He would not have the authority to announce, on behalf of God, liberation. That is why we wanted to emphasize in the same speech at the opening of the Synod "the need to clearly reaffirm the specifically religious purpose of evangelization. The latter would lose its reason for being if it deviated from the religious axis that directs it: above all the kingdom of God, in its fully theological sense."
33. Regarding the liberation that evangelization announces and strives to put into practice, it should rather be said:

34. For this reason, when preaching liberation and associating with those who act and suffer for it, the Church does not admit to limiting its mission to the religious field alone, becoming disinterested in the temporal problems of man; but reaffirms the primacy of his spiritual vocation, rejects the substitution of the proclamation of the kingdom for the proclamation of human liberations, and also proclaims that his contribution to liberation would not be complete if he neglected to announce salvation in Jesus Christ.

35. The Church associates, but never identifies, human liberation and salvation in Jesus Christ, because it knows by revelation, by historical experience and by reflection of faith, that not every notion of liberation is necessarily coherent and compatible with an evangelical vision of man, things and events; that it is not enough to establish liberation, create well-being and development for the kingdom of God to arrive.

36. The Church certainly considers important and urgent the construction of more humane, more just, more respectful of the rights of the person, less oppressive and less overwhelming structures; but he is aware that even the best structures, the most idealized systems soon become inhuman if the inhuman inclinations of man are not healed if there is no conversion of heart and mind on the part of those who live in those structures or govern them.

37. The Church cannot accept violence, especially the force of weapons – uncontrollable when unleashed – nor the death of whoever it may be, as a path to liberation, because it knows that violence inexorably generates new forms of oppression and slavery, sometimes more serious than those from which it seeks to liberate. "We urge you - we already said during our trip to Colombia - not to put your trust in violence or revolution; this attitude is contrary to the Christian spirit and can even delay, instead of favoring, the social elevation to which you legitimately aspire." "We must say and reaffirm that violence is neither Christian nor evangelical, and that abrupt or violent changes in structures will be deceptive, ineffective in themselves and certainly not in accordance with the dignity of the people."

38. Having said this, we rejoice that the Church becomes increasingly aware of its own, essentially evangelical, way of collaborating in the liberation of men. And what does it do? It tries to raise more and more Christians who are dedicated to the liberation of others. To these "liberating" Christians he gives an inspiration of faith, a motivation of brotherly love, a social doctrine to which the true Christian must not only pay attention, but must put it as the basis of his prudence and his experience to translate it concretely into categories of action, participation and commitment. All of this, without being confused with tactical attitudes or service to a political system, must characterize the action of the committed Christian. The Church strives to always insert the Christian struggle for liberation into the global plan of salvation that it itself announces.

39. From this just liberation, linked to evangelization, which seeks to achieve structures that safeguard human freedom, the need to ensure all the fundamental rights of man cannot be separated, among which religious freedom occupies a position of primary importance. We have recently spoken about the current relevance of an important aspect of this issue, highlighting how "many Christians, even today, precisely because they are Christians or Catholics, live suffocated by systematic oppression. The drama of fidelity to Christ and freedom of religion, although alleviated by categorical declarations in favor of the rights of the person and human sociability, continues."
40. The evident importance of the content should not make us forget the importance of the methods and means of evangelization.

41. First of all, and without the need to repeat what we have already recalled before, we must underline this: for the Church the first means of evangelization consists of a testimony of an authentically Christian life, given to God in a communion that nothing should interrupt and at the same time equally consecrated to one's neighbor with unlimited zeal. "Contemporary man listens more willingly to those who bear witness than to those who teach," we recently said to a group of lay people, "or if they listen to those who teach, it is because they bear witness." Saint Peter expressed it well when he exhorted us to live a pure and respectful life, so that if anyone rebels against the word, he may be won over by conduct. It will be above all through her conduct, through her life, that the Church will evangelize the world, that is, through a lived testimony of fidelity to Jesus Christ, of poverty and detachment from material goods, of freedom from the powers of the world, in a word of holiness.

42. It is not superfluous to underline below the importance and necessity of preaching: "But how will they call on Him in whom they have not believed? And how will they believe without having heard of Him? And how will they hear if no one preaches to them?... Therefore, faith comes from hearing, and hearing, through the word of Christ." This law enunciated one day by Saint Paul retains all its force today.

43. This evangelizing preaching takes very diverse forms, which zeal would suggest how to constantly renew. In fact, there are countless events in life and human situations that offer the opportunity to announce, in a discreet but effective way, what the Lord wishes to say in a given circumstance. A true spiritual sensitivity is enough to read God's message in events. Furthermore, at a time when the liturgy renewed by the Council has greatly valued the "liturgy of the Word", it would be a mistake not to see in the homily a valid and very suitable instrument for evangelization. It is true that one must know and put into practice the demands and possibilities of the homily so that it acquires all its pastoral effectiveness. But above all you have to be convinced of it and dedicate yourself to the task with love. This preaching, inserted in a unique way in the Eucharistic celebration, from which it receives a particular strength and vigor, certainly has a special place in evangelization, to the extent that it expresses the deep faith of the sacred minister who preaches and is impregnated with love. The faithful, gathered to form an Easter Church that celebrates the feast of the Lord present in their midst, expect much from this preaching and draw fruit from it as long as it is simple, clear, direct, comfortable, deeply rooted in evangelical teaching and faithful to the Magisterium of the Church, animated by a balanced apostolic ardor that comes from its own character, full of hope, fortifying of faith and source of peace and unity. Many communities, parish or otherwise, live and are consolidated thanks to the homily each Sunday, when it combines these qualities.

44. Regarding evangelization, a means that cannot be neglected is catechetical teaching. Intelligence, especially when it comes to children and adolescents, needs to learn through systematic religious teaching the fundamental data, the living content of the truth that God has wanted to transmit to us and that the Church has sought to express in an increasingly perfect way throughout history. No one will think of doubting that this teaching must be given with the aim of educating customs, not to remain on a merely intellectual level. With all certainty, the effort of evangelization will be greatly beneficial, at the level of catechetical teaching given in the church, in schools where possible or in any case in Christian homes, if catechists have at their disposal appropriate texts, updated wisely and competently, under the authority of the bishops. The methods must be adapted to the age, the culture, the capacity of the people, always trying to fix in the memory, the intelligence and the heart the essential truths that must permeate the entire life. Above all, it is necessary to prepare good catechists – parish catechists, instructors, parents – eager to perfect themselves in this superior, indispensable and demanding art that is religious teaching. For the rest, without needing to neglect in any way the formation of children, it has been observed that current conditions make catechetical teaching more urgent every day in the form of a catechumenate for a large number of young people and adults who, touched by grace, little by little discover the figure of Christ and feel the need to surrender to Him.
45. In our century influenced by the media of social communication, the first announcement, catechesis or the subsequent deepening of faith cannot do without these media, as we have said before.

46. For these reasons, in addition to what we could call the collective proclamation of the Gospel, this other transmission from person to person retains all its validity and importance. The Lord has practiced it frequently - as proven, for example, by the conversations with Nicodemus, Zacchaeus, the Samaritan woman, and Simon the Pharisee - and the Apostles have done the same. Ultimately, is there another way to communicate the Gospel other than to transmit one's own experience of faith to another? The urgency of communicating the Good News to the masses of men should not make us forget that form of announcing through which the personal conscience of man is reached and the influence of a truly extraordinary word that he receives from another man is left there. We can never sufficiently praise priests who, through the sacrament of penance or through pastoral dialogue, show themselves willing to guide people along the path of the Gospel, to encourage them in their efforts, to lift them up if they have fallen, to always assist them with discretion and availability.

47. However, it cannot be overemphasized that evangelization is not limited to the preaching and teaching of a doctrine. Because it must lead to life: to natural life to which it gives a new meaning thanks to the evangelical perspectives that it opens to it; to supernatural life, which is not a denial, but purification and elevation of natural life. This supernatural life finds its living expression in the seven sacraments and in the admirable fruitfulness of grace and holiness they contain.

48. With this we are touching on an aspect of evangelization that cannot leave us insensitive. We now want to refer to that reality that is usually designated nowadays by the term popular religiosity.

49. The last words of Jesus in the Gospel of Mark give evangelization, which the Lord entrusts to the Apostles, a universality without borders: "Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature."

50. Throughout twenty centuries of history, Christian generations have periodically faced various obstacles to this mission of universality. On the one hand, the temptation of the evangelizers themselves to narrow their field of missionary action under different pretexts. On the other hand, the resistance, often humanly insurmountable, of those to whom the evangelizer addresses. Furthermore, we must note with sadness that the evangelizing work of the Church is seriously hindered, if not prevented, by public powers. It happens, even in our days, that the announcers of the word of God are deprived of their rights, they are persecuted, threatened, eliminated just for the fact of preaching Jesus Christ and his Gospel. But we are confident that finally, despite these painful trials, the work of these apostles will not be lacking in any region of the world.

51. Reveal Jesus Christ and his Gospel to those who do not know them: this is the fundamental program that the Church, since the morning of Pentecost, has assumed, as received from its Founder. The entire New Testament, and especially the Acts of the Apostles, testify to the privileged, and in a certain way exemplary, moment of this missionary effort that will later mark the entire history of the Church.

52. Although this first announcement is specifically addressed to those who have never heard the Good News of Jesus or to children, it is becoming increasingly necessary, due to the frequent situations of de-Christianization in our days, for a large number of people who received baptism, but live outside of any Christian life; for simple people who have a certain faith, but know little about its foundations; for intellectuals who feel the need to know Jesus Christ in a different light from the teaching they received in their childhood, and for many others.

53. It also addresses immense sectors of humanity that practice non-Christian religions. The Church respects and esteems these non-Christian religions, as they are the living expression of the soul of vast human groups. They carry within themselves the echo of millennia in the search for God; search incomplete but frequently done with sincerity and righteousness of heart. They have an impressive heritage of deeply religious texts. They have taught generations of people to pray. They are all full of innumerable "seeds of the Word" and constitute an authentic "evangelical preparation", to quote a happy expression of the Second Vatican Council taken from Eusebius of Caesarea.

54. However, the Church does not feel excused from paying equally tireless attention to those who have received the faith and who, sometimes for many generations, remain in contact with the Gospel. In this way it tries to deepen, consolidate, nourish, make more and more mature the faith of those who already call themselves faithful or believers, so that they become more and more so.

55. Equally significant is the concern, present in the Synod, towards two spheres that are very different from each other and yet very close to each other due to the challenge that, each in its own way, they throw at evangelization. The first is what we can call the increase of disbelief in the modern world. The Synod set out to describe this modern world: under this generic name, how many currents of thought, values ​​and countervalues, latent aspirations or seeds of destruction, old convictions that disappear and new convictions that are imposed!

56. A second sphere is that of non-practitioners; a whole multitude, today very numerous, of baptized people who, to a large extent, have not formally renounced their baptism, but are totally outside of it and do not live it. The phenomenon of non-practitioners is very old in the history of Christianity and represents a natural weakness, a great incongruity that hurts us in the depths of our hearts. However, today it presents new aspects. It is often explained by the typical rootlessness of our time. It also arises from the fact that Christians today approach non-believers and constantly receive the influence of unbelief. On the other hand, contemporary non-practitioners, more than those of other times, try to explain and justify their position in the name of an inner religion, autonomy or personal authenticity.

57. Like Christ during the time of his preaching, like the Twelve on the morning of Pentecost, the Church also has before it an immense human multitude that needs the Gospel and has a right to it, since God "wants all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth."

58. The Synod dealt a lot with these "small communities" or "base communities", since they are frequently mentioned in the Church today. What are they and why should they be special recipients of evangelization and at the same time evangelizers?

59. If there are men who proclaim the Gospel of salvation in the world, they do so by command, in the name and with the grace of Christ the Savior. "How will they preach if they are not sent?" wrote one who was undoubtedly one of the greatest evangelizers. No one can do it without being sent.
60. The realization that the Church is sent and has the mandate to evangelize the entire world should awaken in us a double conviction.
61. At this point in our reflection we pause with you, brothers and children, on a particularly important issue in our days.

62. However, this universal Church is in fact incarnated in the particular Churches, made up of this or that portion of concrete humanity, who speak such language, are tributaries of a cultural heritage, of a vision of the world, of a historical past, of a specific human substratum. Openness to the riches of the particular Church responds to a special sensitivity of contemporary man.

63. Particular Churches deeply amalgamated, not only with the people, but also with the aspirations, the riches and limits, the ways of praying, of loving, of considering life and the world that distinguish this or that human group, have the function of assimilating the essential of the evangelical message, of transferring it, without the slightest betrayal of its essential truth, to the language that these men understand, and, after announcing it in that same language.

64. But this enrichment requires that local Churches maintain this clear openness to the universal Church. It must be well noted, moreover, that the simplest, most evangelical Christians, most open to the true meaning of the Church, have a spontaneous sensitivity with respect to this universal dimension; they instinctively and deeply feel their need; They easily recognize themselves in it, they vibrate with it and they suffer deep within themselves when, in the name of theories that they do not understand, they want to impose a church devoid of this universality, a regionalist church, without horizons.

65. Precisely in this sense we wanted to pronounce, at the closing of the Synod, a clear word full of paternal affection, insisting on the function of the Successor of Peter as the visible, living and dynamic principle of unity between the Churches and, consequently, of the universality of the one Church. We also insisted on the serious responsibility that falls upon us, which we share with our brothers in the Episcopate, to keep unchanged the content of the Catholic faith that the Lord entrusted to the Apostles: translated into all languages, clothed with symbols specific to each people, made explicit by theological expressions that take into account diverse cultural, social and also racial means, it must continue to be the content of the Catholic faith as the Ecclesial Magisterium has received and transmits it.

66. The entire Church is therefore called to evangelize and, however, within it we have to carry out different evangelizing tasks. This diversity of services in the unity of the same mission constitutes the richness and beauty of evangelization. Let's remember these tasks in a few words.

67. The Successor of Peter, by the will of Christ, is charged with the preeminent ministry of teaching revealed truth. The New Testament frequently presents Peter "full of the Holy Spirit," speaking on behalf of all. That is why Saint Leo the Great speaks of him as one who has deserved the primacy of the apostolate. For the same reason the voice of the Church presents the Pope "at the culmination âin apex, in speculaâ, of the apostolate." The Second Vatican Council wanted to underline this, declaring that "Christ's mandate to preach the Gospel to every creature ( [+[0]+] ) refers first of all and immediately to the bishops with Peter and under the guidance of Peter."

68. United to the Successor of Peter, the bishops, successors of the Apostles, receive, by virtue of their episcopal ordination, the authority to teach revealed truth in the Church. They are the teachers of the faith.

69. Religious, too, have in their consecrated life a privileged means of effective evangelization. Through their most intimate being, they are situated within the dynamism of the Church, thirsty for the Absolute of God, called to holiness. It is to this holiness that they bear witness. They embody the Church eager to surrender to the radicalism of the beatitudes. Through their lives, they are a sign of total availability towards God, the Church, and their brothers.
70. Lay people, whose specific vocation places them at the heart of the world and at the guide of the most varied temporal tasks, must therefore exercise a unique form of evangelization.

71. Within the evangelizing apostolate of the laity, it is impossible not to emphasize the evangelizing action of the family. She has well deserved, at different times in history and at the Second Vatican Council, the beautiful name of "Domestic Church." This means that in each Christian family the various aspects of the entire Church should be reflected. On the other hand, the family, like the Church, must be a space where the Gospel is transmitted and from where it radiates.

72. Circumstances invite us to pay very special attention to young people. Their numerical importance and their growing presence in society, the problems they face must awaken in us the desire to offer them with zeal and intelligence the ideal that they must know and live. But, in addition, it is necessary that young people, well formed in the faith and rooted in prayer, increasingly become apostles of youth. The Church expects a lot from them. For our part, we have frequently expressed the trust we place in youth.

73. This is how the active presence of lay people in the midst of temporal realities acquires all its importance. We must not therefore overlook or forget another dimension: lay people can also feel called or be called to collaborate with their Pastors in the service of the ecclesial community, for its growth and life, exercising very diverse ministries according to the grace and charismas that the Lord wants to grant them.
74. We would not like to end this conversation with our beloved brothers and children, without making a call regarding the interior attitudes that should animate the workers of evangelization.

75. There will never be possible evangelization without the action of the Holy Spirit. On Jesus of Nazareth the Spirit descended at the moment of baptism, when the voice of the Father – "You are my beloved son, in you I put my pleasure" – manifests in a sensitive way his choice and mission.

76. We now consider the very person of the evangelizers. It has been frequently repeated in our days that this century thirsts for authenticity. Especially in relation to young people, it is stated that they suffer horror from what is fictitious, from falsehood, and that they are also decidedly supporters of truth and transparency.

77. The force of evangelization will be greatly weakened if those who announce the Gospel are divided among themselves by so many kinds of ruptures. Is this not perhaps one of the great evils of evangelization? Indeed, if the Gospel that we proclaim appears torn by doctrinal quarrels, by ideological polarizations or by mutual condemnations among Christians, at the whim of their different theories about Christ and the Church, and even because of their different conceptions of society and human institutions, how can we expect that those to whom our preaching is directed do not appear disturbed, disoriented, if not scandalized?

78. The Gospel that has been entrusted to us is also the word of truth. A truth that sets people free and is the only one that seeks peace of heart; This is what people are looking for when we announce the Good News. The truth about God, the truth about man and his mysterious destiny, the truth about the world. Difficult truth that we seek in the Word of God and of which we are not, we repeat once again, neither the owners, nor the arbitrators, but the depositaries, the heirs, the servants.

79. The work of evangelization supposes, in the evangelizer, an ever-growing brotherly love towards those he evangelizes. A model of evangelizer like the Apostle Saint Paul wrote to the Thessalonians these words that are quite a program for us: "Thus, carried away by our love for you, we want not only to give you the Gospel of God, but even our own lives: so loved did you become to us."

80. Our call is now inspired by the fervor of the greatest preachers and evangelizers, whose lives were consecrated to the apostolate. Among them We are pleased to remember those that We Ourselves have proposed for the veneration of the faithful during the Holy Year. They have known how to overcome all the obstacles that stood in the way of evangelization.

81. This is, brothers and children, the cry that springs from our soul, like an echo of the voice of our brothers gathered in the Third General Assembly of the Synod of Bishops. This is the slogan that we want to give ourselves at the end of the Holy Year, which has allowed us to perceive better than ever the needs and expectations of a multitude of brothers, Christians or not, who expect the Word of salvation from the Church.

82. These are the wishes that we are pleased to place in the hands and heart of the Blessed Virgin, the Immaculate, on this day especially dedicated to Her and on the 10th anniversary of the closing of the Second Vatican Council. On the morning of Pentecost, She presided with her prayer at the beginning of evangelization under the influence of the Holy Spirit. May She be the star of the ever-renewed evangelization that the Church, docile to the Lord's command, must promote and carry out, especially in these difficult and hopeful times.
